summary: This document updates IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and its subnet variants so that a node owning or connected to a prefix can register it with neighbor routers. The registration says the prefix is reachable through the node. It updates several RFCs including RFC 4861 and RFC 8505.

plainLanguage.summary: A node can tell nearby routers, "to reach this street, come through me." This is how it registers.

questions: what is the p-field value 3 in earo
how does a 6lr redistribute a registered prefix

subtitle: How a low-power IPv6 node can register a whole prefix with its neighbor routers, not just single addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Subnet Neighbor Discovery lets a constrained node register single addresses with a router, but a node that owns or fronts a whole prefix (for example a border router to a stub network) had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: The Neighbor Solicitation with an Extended Address Registration Option (EARO) gets a new P-Field value of 3 and a 7-bit prefix length from 16 to 120, so the node registers a prefix and can set the R flag to ask the router to redistribute it in whatever routing protocol it runs, such as RPL.
tldr.outcome: A router can now learn that a prefix is reachable via a node without a loop, keep per-registrant state, and route to the registrant with the longest matching prefix, all without the node sending multicast or becoming a router itself.

today: RFC 9926 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2026, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It itself updates RFC 4861, RFC 6550, RFC 8505, RFC 8928 and RFC 9010.

sections.title: Why Prefixes Need Registering
sections.content:
RFC 9926 belongs to a family of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery extensions for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs), where energy is the scarcest resource and radios must sleep most of the time. Classic Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) is reactive and relies on multicast for duplicate address detection and address lookup. Multicast reaches every node on the link even when at most one is the target, and it assumes everyone is awake to hear it.

The 6LoWPAN line of work turns this around. With RFC 6775 and RFC 8505, a node proactively registers its unicast addresses with a router using a unicast Neighbor Solicitation that carries an Extended Address Registration Option (EARO). RFC 9685 added anycast and multicast addresses. RFC 9926 adds the last piece: registering a unicast prefix, up to 120 bits long, instead of an address.

The RFC explains why it extends the EARO rather than using a Router Advertisement with a Route Information Option. That option is not intended to inject routes, lacks control information such as the R flag, and has no equivalent of the Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR), so it cannot be trusted for safe injection into a routing protocol. It also keeps the node from appearing as a router and from using broadcasts or complex state machines.
sections.plainLanguage: Small battery devices want to sleep, not shout at everyone. So instead of asking the whole room, they quietly tell one router what they own. This RFC lets them say they own a whole street of addresses, not just one house.

sections.title: Overview: Who Registers What
sections.content:
The RFC describes a typical RPL-based deployment. One or more 6LBRs (6LoWPAN Border Routers) act as the RPL Root. Intermediate routers pass routing information toward the Root. 6LRs are the routers that serve nodes, and 6LNs are the RPL-unaware nodes that need Subnet Neighbor Discovery to get reachability. A node that implements this RFC MUST also implement RFC 8505, and the RFC introduces no new option: it modifies existing ones.

A 6LN registers a prefix with P-Field value 3 in the EARO. Several 6LNs that act as border routers to the same external network, or as access routers to the same subnet, may register the same prefix with the same 6LR or with different ones. If the R flag is set in the registration of one or more 6LNs for a prefix, the 6LR MUST, according to its redistribution policy, redistribute the prefix in the routing protocols it participates in. How long it does so is based on the longest registration lifetime across the registrations that have not expired.

The RFC names virtual links, shared links and hub links as places this applies. More generally, the 6LN may be a router running a different routing protocol in an external stub network. Prefix registration decouples that protocol from the one the 6LRs run in the main LLN, and signals when to redistribute.

The RFC also defines one new term, Origin: the node that issued the prefix advertisement, either as an NS(EARO) or as a DAO carrying a Transit Information Option and an RPL Target Option.
sections.plainLanguage: The little devices tell a nearby helper router about the streets they look after. If a device says "please tell everyone else," the helper passes the news along for as long as at least one device still says the street is its.

sections.title: Changes to the Messages
sections.content:
The P-Field is a 2-bit field from RFC 9685 that says what kind of thing is being registered. Values 0 to 2 were already taken, and value 3 was the only one left. This RFC assigns it to a unicast prefix. When a router receives an NS(EARO) with the P-Field set to 3, it MUST install a route to the indicated prefix via the source address of the NS(EARO).

In an NS message the EARO Status field is not used, so this RFC repurposes it. It now holds a flag F and a 7-bit Prefix Length. For P-Field 3 the length MUST be in the range 16 to 120. A 7-bit value of 0 is understood as a truncated 128, meaning an address, which keeps the format backward compatible with RFC 8505. In an NA message the field still carries a status.

The EARO F flag (Forwarding) says the prefix is topologically correct through the registering node. The node relays packets whose source address derives from the prefix to the outside, in line with ingress filtering as in BCP 38, and the receiver forwards such packets to the registering node. When F is not set, the node owns the prefix and delivers packets whose destination derives from it. Which side is inside or outside is defined administratively.

In the Target Address field, a node that owns an address derived from the prefix with a non-zero interface ID MUST put one of those addresses there in full. Otherwise it MUST put the prefix padded with zeros.

The EDAR and EDAC messages that a router exchanges with the 6LBR get a matching change. With P=3 they carry a 15-byte Prefix field holding up to 120 bits padded with zeros, followed by a reserved bit and a 7-bit Prefix Length from 16 to 120.

There are two different F flags. One is in the EARO and means forwarding. The other is a new capability bit, "Registration for prefixes supported", in the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option (6CIO). A router sets it to tell nodes that it accepts prefix registrations, will route packets for matching addresses to the registrants, and will redistribute the route if the R flag is set. The IANA registry lists it as bit 16.
sections.plainLanguage: The note a device sends already has a blank space. This RFC writes a number there that says how long the street name is, and a tick box that says whether the device is the owner or just the way out.

sections.title: How Registration Behaves
sections.content:
For the node, registering a prefix looks much like registering an address. The difference is on the router side, which keeps separate state for each origin and merges them when it advertises. The 6LR MUST keep a registration state per tuple of IPv6 prefix, prefix length and ROVR, and it SHOULD notify the 6LBR with an EDAR message unless it knows the 6LBR is legacy. The 6LBR MUST keep state per tuple of prefix and ROVR. Both are extended to accept more than one registration for the same prefix, since several 6LNs may register it.

Duplicate address detection for prefixes and addresses becomes a prefix overlap match. Whether overlapping addresses and prefixes may be registered is a network policy decision. If overlaps are allowed, the longest prefix match wins: the route is installed toward the node that registered with the longest match, all the way down to /128. This is useful when a router registers an aggregate while a host inside it registers its own piece.

A 6LR that is a border router to external prefixes, or owns them, SHOULD register them on all interfaces from which it might relay traffic for them. It MUST set the P-Field to 3 and the R flag to receive the traffic. If a 6LN sets R to ask for redistribution, the 6LR MUST NOT register that prefix with yet another router unless loops are avoided some way, such as following a tree structure.

The "Registration Refresh Request" status also applies to prefixes. A device that may have lost state, for example after a reboot, SHOULD send an asynchronous NA(EARO) with that status to the all-nodes link-scope multicast address (ff02::1), with TID set to 0 and ROVR set to all zeros. Peers then re-register. If the message is resent in quick succession, a node that recently processed one ignores the rest for a configurable period, 10 seconds by default.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps a notebook with one line for every device that claims a street. If two devices claim overlapping streets, the one with the more exact, longer address wins. If a router loses its notebook, it shouts once and everyone tells it again.

sections.title: Redistribution into RPL
sections.content:
RPL (RFC 6550) is the routing protocol used in route-over LLNs. RFC 9010 already lets a 6LR inject a registered address into RPL when R is set. This RFC adds that, on a registration with R set to 1 and P-Field 3, the 6LR injects the prefix using a prefix RPL Target Option whose P-Field MUST be 3. When a packet arrives for an address derived from the prefix, the 6LR delivers one copy as a unicast link-layer frame to exactly one registrant, choosing the best 6LN by longest prefix match.

RFC 6550 uses the Path Sequence to keep only the freshest route. For prefix routes, the Path Sequence is now compared between, and only between, advertisements for the same Target from the same origin, meaning the same ROVR. The comparison cannot apply when the origin is unknown because it did not support this RFC.

A RPL router that merges several advertisements for the same prefix MUST advertise the longest remaining lifetime across all origins. When that lifetime runs out, it sends a no-path DAO with lifetime 0, using the same ROVR as before. That ROVR is the single descendant that advertised the Target, or the router itself if there is more than one.

The RFC also updates RFC 8929, where a 6LBR can proxy registrations. A proxy MUST use the P-Field as received in the EDAR or NS(EARO), and the exact same prefix and prefix length, when it generates the proxied NS(EARO).
sections.plainLanguage: When the helper router hears about a street, it tells the wider road network. If several devices claim the same street, it keeps saying so until the last of them stops. Then it sends a goodbye message.

sections.title: Mixed Networks and Example Topologies
sections.content:
Devices with different levels of support can coexist. A legacy 6LN never registers prefixes, so its service does not change. A legacy 6LR does not set the F capability bit in the 6CIO, so an upgraded 6LN will not register prefixes with it, though it may with other 6LRs that support this RFC. A legacy 6LBR may fail to realize that an EDAR describes a whole prefix and answer "duplicate" in the EDAC status. The 6LR MUST ignore a duplicate status in the EDAR for prefixes.

On a shared link, more than one prefix is deployed over the same layer-2 link. In the RFC's example, 6LR1 provides access to the outside and 6LR2 owns P2::. 6LR2 registers P2:: to 6LR1, which installs a route to P2:: via 6LR2, so addresses derived from P2:: stay reachable. 6LR2 may then use ICMP Redirect to shorten the path. If P2 was delegated by 6LR1, for example with DHCPv6, 6LR1 is expected to aggregate it and R is not needed. Unless 6LR2 knows that, it SHOULD set R.

In a hub link with stub spokes, routers such as 6LR2 and 6LR3 connect stub links to a hub link served by 6LR1. The same registrations make nodes behind each stub router reachable through 6LR1. If 6LR3 and 6LR4 both connect to the same stub link with prefix P3, both may register it to 6LR1, which applies its own load-balancing logic to pick one.
sections.plainLanguage: New and old devices can share a network. Old ones simply do not use the new trick. In bigger setups, a router near the door learns which side-street routers lead to which streets and sends mail the right way.

sections.title: Protecting Who May Register
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8505 also apply. In particular the link layer SHOULD be protected enough to prevent rogue access, otherwise a rogue node with physical access can inject packets and attack from inside.

Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery (AP-ND, RFC 8928) lets a node sign its registrations with a key pair so a router can verify ownership. That does not work with a node-local key pair when several nodes may register the same prefix. If AP-ND is used for a prefix, a key pair MUST be created and tied to the prefix before the prefix is deployed, and a ROVR MUST be generated from it. The prefix and ROVR MUST be installed in the 6LBR at the first registration or by an external mechanism such as IP Address Management (IPAM) or DHCPv6 snooping. The key pair MUST be provisioned in every node that needs to register the prefix or a prefix inside it.

The RFC notes that updating the keys of a prefix in all 6LNs is not clearly documented and may not finish in time on all nodes. Installing a new address with new keys and switching traffic to it when migration is complete may be simpler. Extending the mechanism to anycast and multicast addresses is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: To stop a stranger from claiming your street, the street gets a secret key, and every device allowed to speak for it gets a copy. The router only believes claims that can show the key.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Forwarding flag: the sender expects other routers to forward packets sourced from the prefix to it.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: 16 to 120 when the P-Field is 3; 0 is read as a truncated 128, an address.

fields.name: r
fields.desc: Reserved; set to zero and ignored.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Asks the router to redistribute the registered prefix.
